prompt.context: We are in the 1990s, and you are a consultant working for a respected Private Equity fund interested in consolidating the on-site coin laundry business in the state of Michigan. The client has pre-negotiated acquiring four thousand locations at a multiple of five times their current annual Net Income.
prompt.question: Should the client move forward with the deal?

clarifying_info.q: What investment is available for the turnaround?
clarifying_info.a: The turnaround should be based on a minimal or zero investment strategy, aside from the initial acquisitions.

clarifying_info.q: Does the client have experience in this industry?
clarifying_info.a: The client has no previous experience nor other portfolio companies in the coin laundry business or related businesses.
Highly fragmented. The current largest player manages 3,000 locations and has 3% market share.

clarifying_info.q: How many locations will the client control after the acquisition?
clarifying_info.a: The 4,000 locations will represent 4% market share for the client.

clarifying_info.q: How many total locations exist in Michigan?
clarifying_info.a: There are 100,000 locations in the state of Michigan.

clarifying_info.q: What is the condition of the facilities?
clarifying_info.a: The facilities are often unattractive, unclean, and unorganized.

exhibits.title: Target segment: on-site coin laundry business
exhibits.shows: A diagram showing the laundry industry hierarchy: Laundry industry splits into Laundry shop/Dry cleaning and Coin laundry. Coin laundry splits into Off-site coin laundry and On-site coin laundry. On-site coin laundry (the target segment) is defined as facilities installed in community areas such as student housing, apartment buildings, and hospitals.
exhibits.data: Three-tier taxonomy identifying on-site coin laundry as the target segment.

exhibits.title: On-site coin laundry business Industry Profile
exhibits.shows: A profile of the on-site coin laundry business covering Revenue Model, Operational Model, and Financials sections.
exhibits.data: Revenue Model: target companies own machines, negotiate installation in community areas, receive a share of coin inflow, average revenue split agreement is 50%, agreements renewed annually. Operational Model: companies responsible for all operations; major costs are coin collecting staff, equipment, and maintenance; landlords grant free space in return for revenue share. Financials: cash business, no inventories, no working capital, profit margins 40% of Net Revenues (Gross Revenues less landlord share), virtually no growth expected.

exhibits.title: Demand, Supply, Utilization, and Price
exhibits.shows: A chart showing Demand, Supply, and Utilization (measured in machines in use/demand per hour) plotted against time of day, with Price ($/cycle) also indicated. Peaks and troughs of demand are visible across the day relative to fixed supply.
exhibits.data: Current average utilization: 60%. Peaks of demand occur before and after general working hours. Idle periods exist during other parts of the day. Current price per cycle: $1.5.

exhibits.title: Demand, Supply, Utilization, and Price - New Pricing Model
exhibits.shows: A chart showing the same demand/supply/utilization axes as Exhibit 3 but with a new variable pricing model applied, illustrating the effect of higher prices during peak periods and lower prices during troughs.
exhibits.data: New pricing model impact: average utilization increases by +25%; average price per cycle increases by +20%.

exhibits.title: Revenue Split Agreement Benchmark
exhibits.shows: A benchmark table or chart comparing revenue split agreements across industry players, including the target companies and named competitors.
exhibits.data: Target companies have the worst (lowest) negotiation results in the industry. Competitor A benchmark rate: 60%. Industry average: 70%.

framework: Purchase Price: (Current Gross Revenue) x (Current Profit Margin) x (Negotiated Multiple of 5x Net Income) — estimate current NI first

Potential for revenue improvements: (1) Maximize capacity utilization via pricing strategy; (2) Increase average price via variable/dynamic pricing; (3) Renegotiate revenue split agreements with landlords; (4) Add new low-investment revenue streams (vending machines, laundry supplies dispensers, entertainment)
Potential for cost optimization: economies of scale post-consolidation, adoption of best practices, standardization across 4,000 locations
Investment evaluation: compare total purchase price to incremental annual profit post-turnaround; assess whether payback target of 2 years is met

questions.guidance: Candidate should build up Gross Revenue per location per year from operating parameters, then apply revenue split and profit margin to get Net Income per location, multiply by 4,000 locations and then by the 5x multiple.

math.setup: Revenue per machine per hour = utilization x (60 min / cycle time) x price per cycle. Aggregate to daily, annual, then apply revenue split and margin.
steps: Revenue per machine per hour = 60% utilization x 1 cycle/hr x $1.5 = $0.90/machine/hr
Revenue per machine per day = $0.90 x 19 working hours = $17.10/machine/day
Revenue per location per day = $17.10 x 10 machines = $171/location/day
Gross Revenue per location per year = $171 x 350 days = $59,850 ≈ $60,000
Net Revenue = Gross Revenue x (1 - 50% landlord split) = $240M x 50% = $120M
Net Income = Net Revenue x 40% profit margin = $120M x 40% = $48M
Total annual cost = Net Revenue - Net Income = $120M - $48M = $72M
Purchase Price = Net Income x 5x multiple = $48M x 5 = $240M

questions.prompt: What are the main issues with the current operation, and how can the client increase revenues? (Question 2 — hand Exhibit 3)
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify that demand peaks before and after working hours while supply is fixed, causing unattended demand and low utilization (60%). Because supply is fixed (low-investment strategy) and there is no control over demand timing, the only lever is pricing strategy.

questions.prompt: Propose a new pricing strategy and describe its expected impacts (Question 3).
questions.guidance: Candidate should propose a variable/dynamic pricing model: higher prices during peak demand periods to manage demand and capture value; lower prices during troughs to stimulate utilization. Expected impacts: (1) Demand is very inelastic within a reasonable range — customers prefer on-site convenience over alternatives; (2) Higher price will somewhat negatively impact customer experience but alternatives are much more expensive; (3) Lower off-peak prices increase utilization during idle periods.

questions.prompt: What is the new pricing model's expected impact on revenue? (Question 4 — hand Exhibit 4)
questions.guidance: After candidate identifies the two main impacts — higher capacity utilization and higher average price — provide the estimates: utilization +25%, average price +20%. Candidate should calculate combined revenue impact multiplicatively.

math.setup: Combined revenue impact = (1 + price increase) x (1 + utilization increase) - 1. Apply to base Gross Revenue.

questions.prompt: Analyze the revenue split agreement benchmark (Question 5 — hand Exhibit 5).
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify that the target companies have the worst revenue split agreements in the industry. A conservative renegotiation to match Competitor A's rate of 60% (vs. current 50%) would increase Net Revenues with minimal risk of losing market share. Candidate should confirm the deal attractiveness under this conservative scenario before proposing more aggressive renegotiation toward the 70% industry average.

questions.prompt: How else could you increase revenues? (Question 6 — optional)
questions.guidance: Candidate should brainstorm low-investment ancillary revenue streams that exploit the existing captive customer base in laundry facilities. At end of discussion, provide estimates: Annual revenue from new streams = $60M; Profit margin on new streams = 50%.

math.setup: Net Income from new streams = $60M x 50% = $30M
math.answer: Incremental Net Income from new streams = $30M per year

questions.prompt: Should the client move forward with the deal? Calculate post-turnaround profitability and payback (Question 7).
questions.guidance: Candidate should assemble all turnaround levers: new Gross Revenue after pricing ($360M), renegotiated revenue split (60%), unchanged total cost ($72M), plus new revenue streams ($60M at 50% margin). Calculate new Net Income and compare purchase price to payback target of 2 years.

math.setup: Net Revenue = New Gross Revenue x (1 - new revenue split to landlord). Net Income = Net Revenue - Total Cost + New Stream Net Income. Payback = Purchase Price / Annual Net Income.
steps: New revenue split to client = 60% (landlord receives 40%)
New Net Revenue from laundry = $360M x 60% = $216M
math.answer: Payback ≈ 1.4 years, well within the 2-year target. The client should move forward.

brainstorming.prompt: What are potential low-investment new revenue streams the client could add at the laundry facilities?

categories.name: Laundry Supplies
ideas: Laundry supplies dispensers (detergent, softener) via partnership

recommendation: The client should move forward with the deal. Post-turnaround Net Income of approximately $174M per year against a $240M purchase price yields a payback of roughly 1.4 years, meeting the 2-year financial target.
The turnaround plan is not CAPEX intensive: it relies on variable pricing, renegotiating revenue split agreements, and adding ancillary revenue streams — all minimal or zero additional investment.
risks: Revenue split renegotiations can take up to one year to complete depending on each contract's renewal date, delaying the benefit realization timeline.
Landlords may attempt to claim a share of the new ancillary revenue streams (vending, dispensers, entertainment).
The client has no prior experience in this industry, creating execution and management risk across 4,000 locations.
Demand elasticity assumptions may not hold if pricing increases exceed customer tolerance.
next_steps: Analyze due dates of all current revenue split contracts and create a timetable for renegotiation.
Engage the legal department to review new contracts and ensure ancillary revenue streams are protected from landlord revenue-split claims.
Identify and negotiate with suppliers to install and manage vending machines and dispensers in facilities.
Explore further revenue split improvement toward the 70% industry average.
Identify cost savings opportunities from economies of scale across 4,000 locations.
